extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners, USPTO discipline respondents, and counsel involved in USPTO ethics/discipline matters
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and requirements governing registered patent practitioners' conduct before the USPTO, including withdrawal from representation, signature and filing rules, cooperation with Office investigations, and the sanctions and mitigating/aggravating factors used in disciplinary settlements under 37 C.F.R. § 11.26.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdrawal of representation (37 C.F.R. § 11.116)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must take reasonable steps to timely withdraw from representation; failure to do so can constitute a violation of § 11.116.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Order states Respondent violated 37 C.F.R. § 11.116 by not taking reasonable steps to timely withdraw from 86 pending patent applications. The Order emphasizes that a practitioner who wishes to cease representing clients must timely effectuate withdrawal so as to avoid remaining the practitioner of record and to prevent adverse consequences (e.g., receiving final orders).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural withdrawal filing requirement (37 C.F.R. § 1.36(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner should file a 'Request for Withdrawal as Attorney or Agent and Change of Correspondence Address' (per 37 C.F.R. § 1.36(b)) when withdrawing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent explained he did not file the Request for Withdrawal form because he trusted the foreign representative would retain other counsel; the Order cites failing to comply with § 1.36(b) as an example of not withdrawing in accordance with USPTO patent rules. Practitioners are expected to file the appropriate form to effect withdrawal and change correspondence address when they cease representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to avoid conduct that prejudices the integrity of the USPTO process (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must not engage in conduct adversely affecting the integrity of the USPTO patent application process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order finds Respondent violated § 11.804(d) by failing to withdraw in accordance with § 11.116 and/or USPTO rules (e.g., § 1.36(b)). The provision is applied to conduct that undermines integrity of filings and proceedings (for example, remaining of record while unauthorized filings occur).

rubrics_metrics.name: Signature and authorization rules for filings (37 C.F.R. § 1.33(b)(3) and S-signature practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Only authorized registered practitioners may sign certain practitioner filings; use of an S-signature or filing signed by an unauthorized person violates USPTO rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The show cause orders alleged that Mark Wang (not authorized to practice before the USPTO) inserted the S-signature of registered practitioner Jie Yang on filings. The Final Order notes in 34 replies an officer or manager of a juristic entity applicant signed replies in violation of 37 C.F.R. § 1.33(b)(3). Practitioners must ensure signatures on submissions are by authorized individuals and must not permit unauthorized signature insertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility to monitor and confirm substitution of counsel
rubrics_metrics.description: When a practitioner requests or expects another practitioner to take over representation, the practitioner should follow up to confirm that new counsel has entered an appearance and that withdrawal has been effectuated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent admitted he should have followed up with HYIP to learn he remained the applicant's representative of record and needed to take steps to withdraw. The Order treats failing to follow up (resulting in remaining of record) as a lapse relevant to the withdrawal obligation under § 11.116.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to notify clients of important orders and status (implicit in withdrawal duties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner should notify clients of final orders or other critical developments affecting their applications, particularly when still the practitioner of record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The facts state that final orders terminating proceedings were sent to Respondent (as practitioner of record) and Respondent did not notify the applicants at that time; he later notified them upon withdrawing. Notification of clients of adverse or dispositive actions is an element of taking reasonable steps when withdrawing to avoid foreseeable prejudice to clients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooperation with USPTO inquiries and investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent must cooperate fully with the USPTO in present or future inquiries into third-party entities or persons involved in reviewing, preparing, signing, filing, or arranging filings related to the matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Agreed-Upon Sanction (d) requires Respondent to cooperate fully with the USPTO in inquiries into entities (e.g., foreign representatives or foreign associates, including W&K IP and HYIP) who were involved in the responses to show cause orders. Cooperation may include interviews and providing information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanction: public reprimand and publication
rubrics_metrics.description: The agreed sanction includes a public reprimand and electronic publication of the Final Order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order states Respondent 'shall be and is hereby publicly reprimanded' and requires the OED Director to electronically publish the Final Order at OED's FOIA Reading Room and to publish a notice in the Official Gazette materially consistent with the provided Notice of Reprimand text. The notice summarizes the misconduct, findings, and remedial actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Waiver of rights to seek reconsideration or appeal (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.56, 11.57)
rubrics_metrics.description: As part of the settlement, Respondent agreed to waive rights to seek reconsideration or review of the Final Order under the cited regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order records that Respondent 'has agreed to waive all rights to seek reconsideration of the Final Order under 37 C.F.R. § 11.56, to waive the right to have the Final Order reviewed under 37 C.F.R. § 11.57, and to waive the right otherwise to appeal or challenge the Final Order in any manner.' Such waivers are terms of settlement and affect post-order remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of disciplinary record in future matters (aggravating factor / rebuttal)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office may consider the record of this disciplinary proceeding in future complaints or disciplinary proceedings involving the respondent, including as an aggravating factor or to rebut representations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Agreement states nothing prevents the Office from considering this record: (1) when addressing further complaints or evidence of same/similar misconduct, and (2) in any future disciplinary proceeding against Respondent as an aggravating factor and/or to rebut statements by Respondent. Practitioners should know that settled records may be used against them later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation of costs and settlement terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties to the Agreement will bear their own costs to date and in carrying out the Agreement and Final Order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order expressly provides that each party bears its own costs; settlement terms (including cost allocations) are part of disciplinary resolutions and can affect whether additional monetary penalties or cost-shifting apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating factors relevant to discipline determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors that mitigate discipline include absence of prior disciplinary history, prompt cooperation, candor, acceptance of responsibility, contrition, and remedial steps (e.g., new SOP, ethics training).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Order notes Respondent had no prior USPTO disciplinary matters, attended a voluntary course on ethically terminating attorney-client relationships, implemented a new standard operating procedure regarding withdrawal, was exceptionally forthcoming and cooperative, and demonstrated genuine contrition—each explicitly described as considerations in agreeing to the sanction.
